full_text_source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41540-026-00667-6 (accepted-manuscript PDF via Unpaywall, saved as P005.txt / 10.1038_s41540-026-00667-6.pdf)
findings: SwarmMAP trains a small MLP cell-type classifier by swarm learning (peer-to-peer weight averaging with blockchain-coordinated merging, no central server) across 3 simulated centers (studies) per organ, and tests on a held-out 4th study (leave-one-study-out). Swarm models matched models trained on the pooled 3 studies on average, but fell short for rare or poorly separable classes, and gained little from adding studies: more training studies raised mean weighted F1 only slightly (not significant, 12/12/4 runs). The paper does not do spatial data or histology, and cites scFed (Wang et al.) as earlier federated cell-type annotation; no batch correction is applied in either arm, with the gene panel taken as the union of each site's top 2000 HVGs.
numbers: Heart/lung/breast collections, 4 studies each; 284 donors, 1,956,243 cells before QC; after QC 1,196,647 / 243,031 / 516,565 cells from 144 / 51 / 89 donors. Union HVG features 3516 / 3566 / 3174. Weighted F1 training on 1, 2, 3 studies (Local_1/2/3), heart cell types 0.947/0.957/0.958; heart subtypes 0.961/0.968/0.972; lung types 0.978/0.981/0.982; lung subtypes 0.945/0.954/0.958. Swarm vs pooled-3-study (Local_3) weighted F1: heart types 0.934 vs 0.958, heart subtypes 0.966 vs 0.972, lung 0.982 vs 0.982 and 0.958 vs 0.958, breast types 0.809 vs 0.970 (as printed), breast subtypes 0.808 vs 0.796. Abstract: swarm mean F1 0.907 vs centralized, Mann-Whitney p=0.937; F1 0.93/0.98/0.88 for heart/lung/breast. MLP 128-32 tanh, Adam lr 1e-3, 100 epochs, batch 128, 3 peers, weights averaged at sync events weighted by dataset size. Runtime Local_3 vs Swarm (cell types): heart 631 s vs 2780 s, breast 272 vs 1120 s, lung 138 vs 610 s. Rare classes: respiratory basal cells (n 262/245/50/11) 82% accuracy local vs under 10% swarm at subtype level; F1 falls with class rarity (Gini index, Fig 4, Table 1).
locations: Abstract; Results sections "Machine learning-based cell type prediction", "Cell type annotation improves with cell count" (Fig 4, Table 1), "Swarm learning performance across cell types" (Fig 5); "Swarm learning performance per cell type" (Fig 6); "Runtime comparison" (Supp Table 5); Discussion; Methods: Dataset description, Data preprocessing (HVG union and private union), Experimental design (Fig 1D), Swarm Learning, comparison with scFed (ref 33) and other classifiers.
caveats: Accepted manuscript marked "article in press"; supplementary tables and figures (Supp Table 4 with CIs, Supp Fig 9 on HVG count) not opened. The breast cell-type pair 0.970 vs 0.809 is reproduced as printed and looks inconsistent with the claim of no significant difference, so treat as unverified. Swarm vs pooled comparison is on 3 peers only; the number of sync events and the sync interval were not found in the text read. "Local_k" is training on the pooled k studies (a centralized model), not a single-site model alone. Single-cell RNA, not spatial; tabular input, not an image encoder. Data-scaling gain is small and run-count is small.

full_text_source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.06393 (v2, 20 Jun 2024; saved as arxiv_2406.06393.pdf, P131.txt)
findings: STimage-1K4M is a public collection of paired H&E and sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics assembled from GEO, 10x Genomics and ten manually curated studies: 1,149 slides, 4,293,195 spots, 10 species, 50 tissues. It documents how inconsistently images and coordinates are shared and how cancer, brain and breast dominate (ascertainment bias). The only modelling experiment is contrastive fine-tuning of CLIP and PLIP image encoders against expression on 12 DLPFC slides of one study, evaluated by linear-probe F1 on layer labels, not expression prediction. The authors say fine-tuning on other tissues gave sub-optimal results, which they attribute to batch effects across datasets and to gene names differing between species, so pooled training was limited to a single tissue and species.
numbers: 1,149 slides; 4,293,195 sub-tile images/spots; 10 species; 50 tissues. Slides by platform: 13.1% Spatial Transcriptomics, 86.5% Visium, 0.3% VisiumHD; spots by platform 1.4% / 54.4% / 44.2%. Brain 21.8% (251 slides), breast 17.8% (205 slides), cancer-related 39.7% (456 slides). Sources: 856 GEO datasets from 121 GEO studies, 58 Visium and 4 VisiumHD from 10x, 233 slides from 10 further studies. Pathologist annotations: 9 studies, 71 slides. Experiment: 12 DLPFC slides, 47,681 spots (Maynard 2021), expression compressed to 128 inputs then a 32-d latent, top 100 HVG; linear probe trained on 80% with 5 seeds, results only in Fig 3a (no numeric table in the text). Fine-tuned CLIP/PLIP beat zero-shot CLIP/PLIP but remain below zero-shot UNI.
locations: Sec 1 Introduction; Sec 3 (Curating STimage-1K4M, Fig 1c, slide and spot breakdown); Sec 5 (experiment, Fig 3a-d); Sec 6 Discussion (Limitations paragraph on batch effects and other tissues); Appendix B and the datasheet answers on licence and public source.
caveats: This is arXiv v2, not necessarily the NeurIPS camera-ready. Provides no learning curve over slides or sites, no expression-prediction metric and no federated analysis; it is useful for Q2 and Q9 as an inventory of public paired data (supports leave-one-study-out simulation) and for Q4 as the authors' own statement that cross-dataset batch effects hurt pooling. Gene-level overlap handling is only "overlapping genes, then top 100 HVG". Counts are from the paper's text and may differ from the current GitHub release. Data are public, so no privacy information.

findings: FedProx modifies FedAvg by adding a proximal penalty (mu/2)||w - w_t||^2 to each client's local objective and by accepting inexact, variable amounts of local work instead of dropping slow clients; the convergence theory rests on a bounded "B-local dissimilarity" assumption and covers non-convex, non-IID cases with partial client participation. Experiments on synthetic data and four small benchmarks (MNIST, FEMNIST, Shakespeare, Sent140) show it stabilises training as heterogeneity grows, while for IID data the term slows convergence and mu should be small or adaptive. It is a general optimiser for iterative nonlinear heads and fine-tuning; it was not tested on omics or imaging.
numbers: Table 1 sizes: MNIST 1,000 devices / 69,035 samples; FEMNIST 200 / 18,345; Shakespeare 143 / 517,106; Sent140 772 / 40,783. 10 devices selected per round on every dataset. Synthetic data generated with heterogeneity parameters alpha, beta in {(0,0),(0.5,0.5),(1,1)} plus IID. Stragglers 0%, 50%, 90%; E=20 local epochs. Best mu from {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}: 1, 1, 1, 0.001, 0.01 for the five federated datasets in Fig 1. Headline: FedProx raises absolute test accuracy over FedAvg by 22% on average in highly heterogeneous settings (90% stragglers). Adaptive mu heuristic: +/-0.1 (Fig 3).
locations: Sec 3.2 and Algorithm 2 (method); Sec 4.1-4.2 Theorem 4 (convergence, B-dissimilarity); Sec 5.1 Table 1 (datasets); Sec 5.2 Fig 1 (stragglers); Sec 5.3 Figs 2-3 (statistical heterogeneity, choice of mu); Appendix C for details (only skimmed).
caveats: Main text read in full; proofs and Appendix C results were not read in detail. Evidence is on classification and language tasks with models of modest size, with rounds and loss as the outcome, not accuracy against pooled training; no personalisation or differing feature sets (gene panels) across clients. Gains are measured against FedAvg with dropped stragglers, so the 22% is not a federated-versus-pooled gap. mu needs tuning per dataset.

full_text_source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.04977 (121-page arXiv version; saved as arxiv_1912.04977.pdf, P273.txt)
findings: The survey separates cross-device from cross-silo federated learning and gives a taxonomy of non-IID data (feature skew, label skew, concept drift and shift, quantity skew), noting that real datasets mix these. For heterogeneity it lists personalisation by featurization, multi-task learning (MOCHA, stateful clients, therefore suited to cross-silo), local fine-tuning, and FedProx-type regularisation, and it states that a customised per-client model can turn heterogeneity into an advantage. On privacy it frames threats by actor (client, server, analyst, outsider), recommends layering secure aggregation/MPC/TEE with differential privacy, notes that DP noise can cause a large accuracy loss at moderate budgets when data are scarce, and says user-level DP trade-offs are poorly understood. In the cross-silo setting it flags hospital-style frictions: data normalisation, labelling, jurisdictions and approval processes.
numbers: No experiments of its own. Cross-silo setting is a few, reliable, addressable clients (Table 1). Federated transfer learning formulation limited to 2 clients (Sec 2.2). Local SGD non-IID bound: needs K below T^(1/3)/N instead of T/N^3 for IID (Sec 3.2.2). Central DP training: clip L2 norm of client updates, add Gaussian noise to the aggregate, track budget with the moments accountant (Sec 4.3.2).
locations: Sec 2.2 (cross-silo, horizontal vs vertical partitioning, federated transfer learning, DP in cross-silo); Sec 3.1 and 3.1.1 (non-IID taxonomy and strategies); Sec 3.2.2 (non-IID convergence, FedProx); Sec 3.3.1-3.3.3 (personalisation); Sec 4.1 (actors and threat models); Sec 4.3.1-4.3.2 (auditing, central DP); Sec 7.5 (cross-silo system challenges); Table 1.
caveats: A 121-page survey: I read the sections above in full and only searched the rest (secure aggregation 4.2, poisoning 5, fairness 6, compression 3.5 not read closely), so read_level is full text for the relevant sections, not every page. It contains no biomedical numbers and no gradient-inversion experiments; for attack evidence on expression or images it points to the literature rather than reporting results. Published in 2021 and does not cover foundation-model fine-tuning or parameter-efficient adaptation.

full_text_source: bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/2023.07.26.550615 (posted 29 Jul 2023), the only copy returned by Unpaywall; saved as 10.1093_database_baaf016.pdf, P292.txt. The published Database 2025 article was not opened.
findings: Across several classifiers and datasets (MNIST variants, fashion MNIST, three AML transcriptome cohorts, kinase fingerprints, cardiac MRI) federated averaging reaches about the same final accuracy as centralised training, including under sample and class imbalance, but only with matched learning rate and batch size (for linear models the federated rate is about N times the central one). The failures matter for this project: federated GBDT broke down under strong class skew, and a federated neural network on the AML cohorts broke down when one cohort was RNA-seq and two were microarray until each gene was z-scored locally before a federated PCA, which is the paper's evidence that platform batch effects hit federated training as in pooled training but are harder to see. Real multi-study splits showed greater variance than simulated splits.
numbers: AML transcriptome: three cohorts A1-A3, about 11,500 patients, 12,709 genes; A1 and A2 microarray, A3 RNA-seq; all classifiers fail above chance on raw genes, so PCA to 100 components via federated PCA was used. Three clients, each one cohort. Federated NN fails on raw A1-A3, recovers with local per-gene z-scoring (Fig 3b vs 3c). Learning-rate relation: federated rate 0.5 about equals central 0.05 with 10 clients (Fig 1a). Cardiac MRI task: ResNet-34, 4 hospital clients. Kinase task: 3 studies as clients (KDR, ABL1). AUC of accuracy curve used as convergence metric; four repeats per classifier. Accuracy values are in Supplementary Table 4, which was not available in the file.
locations: Results (Fig 1 MNIST2/MNIST4, Fig 2 fashion MNIST, Fig 3 AML, Fig 4 kinase, Fig 5 MNM cardiac MRI); sections "Experiments on high dimensional data" and "Usage of heterogeneous datasets highlights the need to think federated"; Discussion; Methods 4.2-4.3 (only skimmed).
caveats: Source is the preprint, not the published version; numbers and conclusions may differ in the final paper. Supplementary tables (accuracy values) not in the file, so no per-arm numeric accuracy is quoted. Classification only, no regression or imaging-to-expression task. Federated PCA reference is [34] in the preprint (supplementary algorithm 3), which I did not open. Methods section was read only partially.

full_text_source: https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1000167&type=printable (open access PDF via Unpaywall; saved as 10.1371_journal.pgen.1000167.pdf, P315.txt)
findings: Homer et al. show that an individual's presence in a pooled sample can be tested from pooled allele frequencies on a SNP array, even when that person contributes about 1% or less of the DNA. The test compares the distance between the person and the pool with the distance between the person and a reference population, summed across many SNPs. The authors draw the inference that composite statistics such as allele frequency or genotype counts released from association studies do not conceal membership; this motivated the later withdrawal of public aggregate GWAS data and is the foundational membership-inference result behind concerns about releasing summary statistics. The attack is on genotypes, not expression or histology, and needs the target's genome plus a reference panel.
numbers: Simulation (1,423 WTCCC controls): 10,000-25,000 SNPs resolve a person at under 1% of the mixture at p<1e-6; about 25,000 SNPs conservatively for p<1e-6 at under 1%; using all SNPs, under 0.1%. With 50,000 SNPs and probe variance up to 0.01, contributions below 2.5% still resolved at p<1e-6; probe noise has a secondary effect. Experiments: 8 mixtures (A-H) on Illumina 550K, Illumina 450S Duo and Affymetrix 5.0 arrays; equimolar pools of 41 and 47 HapMap CEU individuals; two-person mixtures at 90/10 and 99/1; complex mixtures with 184 individuals at about 0.2% each plus 41 or 47 known individuals at 1% or 0.1%; in all mixtures the identification of contributors was possible (Fig 3).
locations: Abstract and Author Summary; Introduction; Methods (Table 1, mixture constructions, theoretical framework); Results: Simulation (Fig 2a-c) and experimental validation (Fig 3); Discussion (GWAS data sharing, forensic use, likelihood-ratio extension).
caveats: Mixtures were tested on SNP microarrays with genotype-level reference data; transfer to expression summary statistics is an analogy (expression profiles are not genotypes, though eQTL-linked leakage is a separate literature not covered here). It does not quantify defences such as DP. The sentence about GWAS data is in the abstract/author summary; I did not locate a separate dedicated GWAS-attack section in the main text beyond the Discussion.

full_text_source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.02596 (v2, 7 Jul 2018; saved as arxiv_1803.02596.pdf, P339.txt)
findings: The paper studies (epsilon, delta)-differentially private linear regression and proposes AdaSSP, which perturbs the sufficient statistics X^T X and X^T y and uses a privately released smallest eigenvalue of X^T X to choose the ridge parameter, and AdaOPS, a posterior-sampling counterpart. Both adapt to data-dependent quantities and need no bound on the coefficient norm; under a linear Gaussian model the estimate is unbiased up to a bounded event and its covariance is inflated by a term that shrinks as n times epsilon-squared grows, so that for large n the privacy cost vanishes relative to sampling error. This is the closest result in the reading list to a one-round, summary-statistic regression head with a stated accuracy cost of DP; it assumes bounded rows and labels and a design with a minimum-eigenvalue gap.
numbers: AdaSSP noise-calibration rate for the excess empirical risk: d^2 log(1/delta) ||theta*||^2 / (alpha n epsilon^2) (Table 1), requiring only that eigenvalue information be released. Experiments: 36 UCI regression datasets, tables at (epsilon=0.1, delta=min{1e-6,1/n^2}) and (epsilon=1); main-text examples bike n=17,379, d=17; buzz n=583,250, d=77; elevators n=16,599, d=18; housing n=506, d=13 (Fig 3); synthetic linear Gaussian d=10, delta=1/n^2, epsilon in {0.1,1}, n from 1e2 to 1e6 (Fig 4); AdaSSP and AdaOPS outperform existing methods on nearly all 36 data sets (abstract). Plain SSP is unstable for small n. SSP/AdaSSP show a gap at large n from spending part of the budget on the eigenvalue release.
locations: Abstract; Sec 3.2 and Table 1 (algorithms and bounds); Sec 4 Algorithms 1-2 and Theorem 2 (guarantees, linear Gaussian result); Sec 5 Figs 3-4 (UCI and synthetic experiments); Sec 6 Conclusion; Appendix A Tables 3-4 and proofs in Appendix B-C (not read).
caveats: Proofs in appendices not read. The guarantees are for a single trusted data holder releasing noisy sufficient statistics; the paper does not treat multiple sites, so a federated version (each site releasing noisy X^T X and X^T y, or distributed DP) is an extension that the paper does not provide. Requires bounded feature and label norms; features were normalised to unit Euclidean norm in the experiments, and ||Y|| below ||X|| ||theta*|| is assumed. Dimensions here are at most 77, far below the embedding sizes or gene counts of a histology-to-expression head, so the cost at d in the thousands is not demonstrated.

full_text_source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10830108/ (published version; local copy P001_PMC10830108.html already in the reading directory from another reader)
findings: Spatial task (Application 3): ST-Net on 23 breast-cancer patients (30,612 spots, 26,949 genes, 100 um spots) is trained centrally, federated, with plain DP-FL, and with PPML-Omics (decentralised DP with a secret-sharing step); the published Table 2 shows arms that differ, unlike the preprint's near-0.91 MSE for every arm. Federation without noise is slightly worse than central (0.9312 vs 0.9090), plain DP-FL collapses at small budgets, and PPML-Omics approaches the central value only at epsilon_T=5 (0.9301) and is 0.988 at epsilon_T=1. A gradient-inversion (iDLG) attack reconstructs training images from the central model's gradients but is blocked under PPML-Omics.
numbers: Averaged test MSE (lower is better), Table 2: Hist2ST central 0.91053; Hist2Gene central 0.88285; ST-Net central 0.90904; ST-Net+FL 0.93120; +FL+MHE 0.90904; FL+DP epsilon_T=0.1 and 0.5: NA; FL+DP epsilon_T=1: 1557.54465; epsilon_T=5: 1.29931; PPML-Omics epsilon_T=0.1: 3.22789; 0.5: 1.08788; 1: 0.98808; 5: 0.93005. One-sided t tests PPML-Omics vs FL-DP: P=8.06e-29 (epsilon_T=1) and 3.10e-14 (epsilon_T=5). Dataset: 23 patients, 3 H&E images per patient, 256-712 spots per replicate. Application 1 clients effect: PPML-Omics keeps utility with 10 or more clients (Fig 2D).
locations: Results, Application 3 (Fig 4A-C, Table 2, table S13); Fig 2D (clients); Methods (datasets, MSE definition, iDLG); Materials and Methods dataset paragraph (23 patients, 30,612 spots).
caveats: Not among the seven papers I was assigned (it appears in the task text as a reading instruction), read at moderate depth: I located Table 2 and the Application 3 text, not every section; the number of clients in the spatial task was not found in the text I read. MSE is on a normalised scale near 0.9 for the central model, meaning the per-gene signal is weak and the arms differ by little; federation/DP effects are measured on the same 23-patient cohort with a patient split not checked here. The preprint-versus-published difference is stated from the task brief (preprint near 0.91 for all arms); I did not open the preprint to confirm, though a bioRxiv v2 PDF is in the reading directory.
